title: Anthropic Splits From Google, OpenAI Over State AI Safety Bill
content: Anthropic is at odds with other big tech firms over a Massachusetts Senate proposal requiring big AI developers to hire independent evaluators to assess catastrophic risks posed by their models every four months. The Massachusetts proposal could set a new standard for AI regulation, which state legislators across the country are pursuing aggressively even as congressional lawmakers drag their feet on passing federal legislation. The proposal also comes as concerns are mounting about the dangers of rogue AI agents in the wake of the OpenAI–Hugging Face attack, when hundreds of agents figured out how to communicate with each other and coordinate an attack on Hugging Face. Anthropic and safety groups support the AI language in the Senate version of the legislation, which is opposed by companies such as Google and OpenAI. The legislation is tucked into a broader economic development bill before the state upper house. A conference committee of the two Massachusetts chambers is now meeting to finalize the bill, which will determine whether the AI provision advances into the final text. Previous AI-related state bills have established new floors for safety regulation that were later reflected in other states’ efforts. For instance, an Illinois bill passed in May instituted the concept of annual third-party compliance audits. The Massachusetts proposal would likely have a similar impact on other states. It goes further than the Illinois bill by requiring independent evaluations of companies’ models themselves, as well as increasing the frequency of audits. On July 24, after the Massachusetts Senate passed its version, Anthropic head of U.S. state and local policy Cesar Fernandez wrote in a post on X that it “raises the bar on AI safety while ensuring that innovation is able to continue.” Anthropic has previously been a vocal supporter of other state-level AI safety bills. Anthropic is joined by AI safety organizations including Encode and Secure AI Project, which have engaged lawmakers in Massachusetts and recently sent a letter of support to the members of the conference committee, Secure AI Project policy director Scott Wisor told The Information. Meanwhile, OpenAI has voiced its objection to the Massachusetts language. In previously unreported letters sent on Aug. 18 and 19 to the conference committee and Sen. Barry Finegold, who has spearheaded the AI language, OpenAI policy executives wrote that Massachusetts should consider a requirement similar to the Illinois bill, and added that “fragmented oversight” across the country would represent an “unhappy result.” “A confusing jumble of rules will unnecessarily delay getting the most advanced cyber models into the hands of state and local officials before bad actors with their own powerful AI break in and exploit vulnerabilities,” wrote Donnie Fowler, the company’s head of U.S. state policy and partnerships, and Ann O’Leary, its global affairs vice president. In a statement issued after publication, an OpenAI spokesperson said the company supports independent third-party technical assessments but thinks they are “best established at the federal level.” OpenAI and Anthropic are not the only AI giants active on the ground. In an interview with The Information, Finegold said he has also met with representatives from Google and Meta Platforms, though he declined to comment on their conversations. Google is concerned about states setting up additional testing requirements beyond the audits laid out in the Illinois bill, according to a person familiar with the company’s thinking. The lack of standards for testing models creates uncertainty about results, making compliance difficult until those standards are established, the person said. Google has previously withheld products in specific jurisdictions due to regulations—for example, it delayed offering its AI Overviews in many European countries until this summer—raising the possibility that the same scenario could happen with its models across different states. Though most states, including Massachusetts, have wrapped up their legislative sessions for the year, the conference committee’s work reconciling the economic development bill is expected to pick up after Labor Day, according to Finegold and political strategists working in the state. Finegold said he continues to engage with tech companies on the bill. He traveled to California in August to meet with representatives from OpenAI and Anthropic. The companies’ interest in pending legislation from Massachusetts reflects the rising importance of states’ roles in advancing AI policy. While OpenAI has previously advocated for federal preemption of state rules to prevent a fragmented patchwork of laws, it has since softened its position, including backing the Illinois law that included third-party audits. In a July blog post , OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer, Chris Lehane, argued for what he dubbed “reverse federalism,” or states establishing a “shared direction through a common framework.” Some AI safety advocates saw OpenAI’s rejection of the Massachusetts AI provision as backtracking. “This ongoing fight looks an awful lot like regressing to the mean,” Encode founder Sneha Revanur wrote on X in August. In an interview, Encode policy adviser Ben Snyder, who has worked with Massachusetts lawmakers on the bill, said he was optimistic OpenAI would change its position. “They don’t want to be seen as a company that is opposing these measures, and I think for good reason,” Snyder said. Whether other companies, including Google and Meta, will lobby more aggressively against the language remains to be seen. Wisor said he expects to see more opposition emerge in the fall as the conference committee works on the language. Another industry group, the Andreessen Horowitz and Y Combinator–affiliated American Innovators Network, is urging the committee to reject the AI provision. “The Senate bill includes several additional compliance requirements that will create substantial barriers to scaling for small companies while making it more difficult to use open-weight models in the Commonwealth,” Executive Director Jeremy Kudon said in a statement. But even if the AI provision doesn’t make it into the final version of the economic bill, it could reappear as other states take up their own attempts at regulating the sector. On Aug. 30, the California legislature advanced a bill that would establish a framework for independent evaluation organizations, though it doesn’t set up requirements for audits of AI companies. The bill still needs to be signed by Gov. Gavin Newsom. Finegold said he has been in conversations with lawmakers from other states about advancing new legislation. “As the technology evolves, I continue to see each state leapfrogging the other state to make sure that we’re ahead of this,” Finegold said.

title: Google’s (Small) Antitrust Victory and Microsoft’s Azure Shift
content: We had lots of news today, including Microsoft’s decision to start breaking out Azure numbers, and Broadcom projecting bonanza growth in its AI chip business in the next couple of years. Oh, and the Trump administration threw its weight behind OpenAI in its copyright lawsuit against The New York Times Co. We have more on all those below. Meanwhile, you’ve heard of the world’s smallest violin. Google may now be playing the world’s smallest trumpet, having won a major victory in what’s arguably the least important antitrust case out there. That would be the ad tech antitrust lawsuit, the second of the two antitrust cases brought by the Justice Department against Google in recent years, and the second the government won —in theory. But as with the first case—over search—the outcome of this one has gone Google’s way. Its punishment for being a monopoly in both cases is so light as to be meaningless. A year after the arguments over how to remedy Google’s ad tech monopoly—we’re talking about the Google ad tools used to sell ad space on independent websites—were heard in a Virginia court, Judge Leonie Brinkema issued a tantalizingly brief ruling on Wednesday. She rejected the government’s proposal for “structural remedies”—that is, forcing Google to divest its ad tech businesses—and accepted most of the proposed “behavioral remedies.” In other words, Google can keep its toys but will have to play nicer with others. Big whoop. These toys aren’t worth much—and their value is degrading by the day. The proportion of ad dollars flowing to independent websites was never great (Google search and YouTube as well as Meta Platforms and Amazon swallow up most ad dollars, after all), and it is shrinking steadily. Some of that is due to AI changes Google made to its search engine, which have reduced the traffic going to websites. But some of it is also that ad money is shifting to video-streaming and mobile apps, two ad markets Google does not dominate. (We explained in this story that Google’s ad tech has fallen behind rivals in those markets.) By the numbers, Google’s network ad revenue—which reflects the ad tech business—accounted for just 9% of its ad revenue in the second quarter (and that’s before Google forks over a majority share to the websites). In 2018, network ads accounted for 17% of total advertising. (Much of the evidence presented by the government stemmed from the 2010s, not the present day.) We don’t know the reasons for Brinkema’s ruling, as the full text won’t be released for a couple of weeks, but during the trial last year , she asked whether forcing Google to divest its ad tech businesses could hurt independent websites. It’s a good bet Brinkema took that into account, just as the judge who heard the search antitrust case took into account AI’s impact in deciding how Google should change its ways. Google’s defense was, in fact, that the open web ad market was in decline. It seems the judge listened. All this is a reminder of the flaws inherent to antitrust enforcement of the tech industry, given how quickly technology-driven markets evolve and how slowly antitrust cases take to wind through the courts. Microsoft’s Idea of Transparency Finally! Microsoft is overhauling how it reports its business segments and will start reporting revenue for its Azure cloud unit quarterly, the software giant said on Wednesday. That’s a big deal. Azure is core to Microsoft’s AI business, so we’ll finally get a better picture of how the company is benefiting from AI. It also means we can compare the big three cloud firms, as both Amazon and Google were already reporting revenue for their cloud units. In the June quarter, for instance, we now know that Amazon Web Services generated $42 billion, Azure generated $29.4 billion and Google Cloud, $24.7 billion. But hold the applause. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said the changes in segment reporting aimed to provide “increased transparency to investors.” Anytime a CEO says something about increasing transparency, you know things are about to become more opaque. In this case, the changes make it harder to figure out the profit margins on Microsoft’s individual segments. That’s because Microsoft is collapsing three segments into two. It is putting into one segment both Azure and its Microsoft 365 cloud software businesses, which it previously reported in separate segments. We used to see operating margins for those separate segments—the one with Azure had an operating margin of 41% in the fourth quarter, while the one that included Microsoft 365 had a margin of 58%. In the future, we’ll see revenue for individual units like Azure but not their operating income. That suggests we’re likely to see an operating profit that reflects both cloud and software, making it harder to figure out how the profits of both are separately changing. That’s not ideal. Microsoft’s pitch, though, is that both the Microsoft 365 and Azure units are sharing AI chips and cloud computing capacity, and that argues in favor of treating them as one segment for reporting purposes. In other words, investors won’t have to worry about how Microsoft is dividing up the chips. Fair enough, we guess. Trump Finds New Way to Attack the News Media President Donald Trump’s attacks on the news media are legendary, including defamation lawsuits and calls for TV networks to lose their license over coverage he doesn’t like. But on Wednesday, the Trump administration came up with a new tactic to undermine the news industry. The Justice Department on Wednesday filed a brief with the court hearing The New York Times Co.’s copyright infringement lawsuit against OpenAI, arguing that training AI models on copyrighted material—the core of the Times’ case—doesn’t violate copyright laws. The administration argued that if the Times prevailed, its approach to copyright could hurt the AI sector, which wouldn’t be good for the country. “Rules of law that make it significantly more difficult to develop a robust AI industry in the United States therefore threaten national security and give a competitive advantage to foreign adversaries who are not so encumbered,” the government argued. We wouldn’t want “rules of law” to get in the way of anything! In Other News • Broadcom CEO Hock Tan projected that the AI chip designer would double AI revenue to $115 billion in 2027 and potentially double it again to $230 billion in 2028. He made the projections as Broadcom reported 86% higher revenue of $29.6 billion in the quarter ending Aug. 2, a sign that its business helping design AI chips for companies such as Google, Meta and OpenAI is continuing to explode ( more here ). • Uber is laying off 10% of its workforce, or about 3,400 people, in an effort to streamline the organization by reducing management layers. In making the announcement , Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi told staffers that “the vast majority” of remote employees needed to move to an office, reducing the proportion of people who can work fully remotely to about 1%. • Anthropic co-founder Tom Brown called on countries to build more data centers at the G20 Innovation Ministerial in North Carolina on Wednesday, arguing that adding more computing power would be the best way for governments to benefit from AI gains. He also praised President Trump’s “let data reign” post on Truth Social earlier this week. • World Labs, a startup led by Stanford University Professor Fei-Fei Li, on Tuesday unveiled Atlas, a new world model that can generate and modify photorealistic, interactive virtual environments based on text, image and video prompts. • The Supreme Court may wade into a battle between state lawmakers and prediction markets companies after New Jersey regulators filed a petition with the highest U.S. court to rule on whether sports bets offered by startups like Kalshi and Polymarket fall outside state gambling regulations. • Anthony Armstrong, former chief financial officer at SpaceX’s xAI, is joining Coinbase’s board, Coinbase said. • Nscale is telling prospective investors it has about $103 billion of total contracted revenue after clinching a $45 billion computing deal with Anthropic, ahead of an initial public offering for the neocloud that could take place as soon as this month, according to documents shared with investors and reviewed by The Information. • Shares of Snowflake rose more than 20% late Wednesday after the database provider surpassed its earlier forecast for product revenue—its most closely watched sales metric—by more than $70 million for the second quarter ending July 31. More here. • Meta Platforms announced Wednesday that it’s rolling out another AI model, Muse Spark 1.3. More here. title: Startups Gravitate to a New, Pentagon-backed Battery to Bypass China’s Chokehold
content: In 2024, the U.S. approved the sale of attack drones to Taiwan, triggering a furious response from China. In retaliation, Beijing blocked the sale of batteries to Skydio, the largest U.S. maker of drones, creating a supply crunch for the company because it had no alternative source of batteries. Beijing’s move, leveraging China’s vast dominance of the world’s battery industry and the supply chain behind it, created worry in Washington and across U.S. businesses. It demonstrated China’s capacity to effectively shut down individual companies, whole industries and some weapons systems. Two years later, SAE International, the standards-setting organization, has released the first formal industry standard for drone batteries. The standard brings uniformity to the dimensions of batteries that power the small drones used most frequently in Ukraine and other war zones. Most Chinese drone batteries are metal cylindrical cells; the new SAE standard version is a flat, rectangular or square battery called a pouch cell. The moves, resembling Thomas Edison’s standardization of the light bulb with the Edison screw, which remains the most common threaded socket, could help juice the small U.S. battery industry by defining the basic building block of drone power systems. If drone makers embrace the standard, battery startups would face lower capital expenses, since it would simplify the cost of setting up and operating a factory. Numerous U.S. battery makers, expecting this drone demand, have already made plans to produce such standard batteries. The standard will also get a boost from the Department of Defense, which backed the effort and appears likely to adopt the standard for the Drone Dominance Program, under which the Pentagon seems likely to eventually buy millions of drones per year. “We want to build an industry outside of China,” said Lisa King, vice chair of the SAE committee that handled the standardization, and head of advanced battery strategy for Leap Manufacturing, a consultancy. King told me that not long after the Chinese blacklisting of Skydio in October 2024, she was leading a battery industry conference in Dayton, Ohio, at which she got into a conversation with an executive from the company. The executive related Skydio’s battery trouble in China and his search for an alternative supply. Skydio was using the Chinese cylindrical cell, known as the 2170 because of its dimensions—21 millimeters in diameter and 70 in length—in addition, in some drones, to a flat pouch cell. The executive was seeking a Western version of the  pouch version. After the conference, King spoke with a Pentagon official whose unit in part funded Leap, the consultancy where she works. This official suggested the standardization effort to bypass China’s battery chokehold, noting that pouch cells were increasingly popular with drone startups for the accommodation of next-generation battery chemistries; such batteries weighed less than the 2170s, a crucial factor in aviation. With the Pentagon’s blessing, King, starting in February last year, began holding conference calls with a group of around two dozen Western companies to decide what the standard should be. The result, in July, was the standard announced by the SAE : The new standard pouch cell would be roughly the same size as the incumbent 2170s when the 2170s were used in groups of six, as is typical in drones. “It is really, really risky to have one single point [of] failure, and that is China, for something as important as power sources,” King said. “Ninety percent of power cells are made in China.” Several battery makers already have plans to make the standard cell. Jaehee Sweeney, chief business development officer at South Korea’s BEI, said the next-generation lithium-metal battery maker already makes one battery that fits the standard and intends to add others. Tom Stepien, CEO of Amprius Technologies, said the silicon battery startup would use the standard cell in an ultrahigh-energy battery it will release in the fourth quarter. The battery will deliver energy density of 500 watt-hours per kilogram, almost twice that of conventional lithium-ion batteries, substantially increasing flight time, Stepien said. Adrian Yao, CEO of Indiana-based battery maker EnPower, told me that even before the SAE standard had been finalized, he began retooling the company’s factory to make more than 2 million of the new pouch cells annually, starting in the middle of next year. He said EnPower has no firm contracts for the batteries but expects them to emerge. He predicts that more battery makers in the U.S. and South Korea will make the standard cell. Drones will not be their only use: “I’m evangelizing this form factor as well for applications like industrial robots, [ranging from the] nonhumanoid to the humanoid,” Yao said. “This is a world in which pouch cells are better than cylindrical cells.” Yao said standardization solves one of the largest problems of getting a battery factory going. When a customer wants to fiddle with a battery’s chemistry or the thickness of the electrodes, it’s no big deal. But changing the dimensions of a cell, even slightly, can involve monstrous cost increases because replacing the manufacturing equipment can cost $30 million. Fixing the dimensions gets rid of that uncertainty. “If we want low costs, if we want to compete, we have to standardize,” he said.

title: Why I’m Launching The Information’s AI Show, AI Deep Dive
content: The Information has become the most trusted source on the AI business by breaking news about the biggest deals in the industry. Now we’re expanding that coverage with a new show called “AI Deep Dive” that will give you a more sophisticated understanding of the technology itself. “AI Deep Dive” will complement our daily coverage with long-form conversations with the researchers and founders working on the frontier of AI. I’m your host. I’ve written about AI at The Information for the past two years, taking advantage of my technical background to uncover and translate highly technical stories in AI and robotics. I studied computer science in college, briefly worked as a programmer and received a crash course in AI research while working at MATS, a mentorship program for AI safety researchers. These days I keep up with AI research in part by discussing a new machine learning paper every week with a reading group. That experience sets me up to guide technical conversations with our guests. To kick off the series, I’ll be talking to Noam Brown, a research scientist at OpenAI, about the challenges involved in creating AI agents that can autonomously take actions on a computer. Each of the following episodes will break down a hard problem on the technological frontier, from training AI models to control robots to studying the neuroscience of their “brains.” As AI barrels ahead, bringing new developments every week, separating hype from real progress has never been more valuable. Understanding which technical problems have researchers stumped and what makes those problems so hard is the best inoculation against the hype. TITV will remain our home for daily coverage of the biggest stories in tech. If you want to better understand the technology behind the business, I hope you’ll tune in when the first episode of “AI Deep Dive” airs on Sept. 14.

title: Why Regulators Are Scrutinizing Prediction Markets' Trading Arms
content: Fast-growing prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket are well known for their consumer apps, where people can bet on everything from sports and elections to the weather and stock prices. But those companies do more than operate consumer apps. Behind the scenes, several prediction markets operate their own exchanges and clearinghouses for the contracts, and some even have trading firms that make bets using the same contracts that are available to customers. Those kinds of setups have caught the attention of U.S. regulators, which have been examining potential conflicts of interest in recent years following the 2022 collapse of crypto exchange FTX and its Alameda Research trading arm. The FTX implosion highlighted the crypto firm’s entanglements between in-house trading and its exchange. Those functions are generally kept separate in traditional financial markets—stock exchanges, for example, typically don’t own the market makers trading on them. More recently, the CFTC has included prediction markets in that scrutiny. The Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which oversees prediction markets including Kalshi and Polymarket US, is now seeking comments on proposed rules aimed at preventing exchanges from giving affiliated trading firms an advantage over customers. They would require trading and exchange businesses to operate independently and would bar the trading firms from making speculative bets against customers. “It’s really to address a different type of market structure that’s being used by crypto and prediction markets,” said Gabe Rosenberg, a partner at Davis Polk who advises financial institutions. “It’s about how many functions in the market can be done by one affiliated group and what protections need to be in place.” Though the rules would apply across U.S. derivatives markets, the CFTC highlighted prediction markets as an area with recent “practical significance.” The agency said it knows of at least six exchanges that allow trading by affiliated firms, which can be a significant source of liquidity for prediction markets. The CFTC comment period ends in early October, after which the agency could revise the proposal and move toward final rules. For now, some of the most popular prediction markets say their setups provide a level playing field for customers, and any affiliated trading firms are market makers that provide liquidity so contracts can trade easily. In the case of Polymarket, a company spokesperson said it doesn’t have its own market maker, either for its U.S. platform or for its separate, blockchain-based platform for international users. Kalshi, which is the biggest U.S. prediction market and is close to raising fresh cash at a $40 billion valuation , operates its own exchange and also owns Kalshi Trading, which trades on that exchange. A Kalshi spokesperson said the company supports the CFTC’s efforts. “Kalshi Trading is unprofitable and represents a very small percentage of our volume. This is a very common and regulated practice in our industry,” the spokesperson said. Kalshi Trading doesn’t receive preferential treatment and doesn’t share personnel, office space or communication channels with Kalshi, the spokesperson said. “Like any financial market, including the stock market, market makers are industry standard because they help bootstrap liquidity,” the Kalshi spokesperson said. Institutional market makers, including outside trading firms as well as Kalshi Trading, represent less than 5% of volume on the exchange’s most liquid contracts, the spokesperson said. Robinhood until recently relied on outside exchanges, including Kalshi’s. Last year, it invested in Rothera, a joint venture exchange between Robinhood and trading giant Susquehanna International Group, with each holding a 45% stake. Robinhood has since been routing some customers’ orders to the new exchange, and Susquehanna makes markets on the exchange. “In compliance with CFTC regulations, we provide a level playing field with fair, transparent and impartial access for all participants,” a Rothera spokesperson said. The rule proposal comes at a time when prediction betting is starting to resemble serious Wall Street markets, drawing outside market makers and sophisticated traders looking to profit from shifting odds. Prices on prediction contracts can change constantly, especially around short-term outcomes such as who will win the next set of a U.S. Open match. In its rule proposal, the CFTC noted concerns that prediction firms could give their own trading operation preferential treatment over other traders or access to nonpublic information. That could put everyday traders and other market participants at a disadvantage, the CFTC said. Under the proposed rules, an exchange would need to disclose any affiliated trading firm and keep its office space, personnel and information systems separate from those of the exchange. Any exchange that offers an incentive program to affiliate trading firms would have to ensure that unaffiliated members can participate on equally favorable terms. The exchanges also can’t give preferential treatment to affiliated firms under the proposal. For instance, if an independent trader puts in a buy or sell order at a given price, the exchange would have to fill their order first even if an affiliated firm placed the same order earlier. Affiliated trading firms wouldn’t be allowed to make directional bets and would need to put in both buy and sell orders for contracts rather than just taking a one-sided position. The CFTC’s focus on the affiliated trading firms comes amid separate regulatory battles prediction markets are facing over the sports-related trading that makes up the bulk of their trading activity. Kalshi, Polymarket and others are under scrutiny over whether their sports contracts are unregistered gambling offerings that should be subject to state-level registrations. Part of the firms’ argument that prediction markets should fall under federal rather than state regulation’ is that, unlike sportsbooks, they don’t trade against customers and are merely matching orders. The fact that some prediction markets also have affiliated trading firms arguably undercuts that logic. Even if the firms are simply market makers providing liquidity, they’re nonetheless taking the other side of customers’ bets on each trade. That underlines the challenge for regulators as they grapple with how prediction markets fit in with existing financial and gambling rules. title: A Decade Ago I Bet Big on China Coverage. I'd Do It Again.
content: I landed in Beijing in March of 2016, Ubered around dozens of tech companies a week and had nightly drinks with Chinese and U.S. investors at the Rosewood in Beijing. On the weekends, I visited the startups that worked Saturdays (they all did) and wandered the malls and parks. I hopped to Hong Kong for some parties and hikes and barely stopped eating! I was in reporting heaven. I was also confused. By my count, there were as many tech reporters covering Uber in San Francisco as there were reporters for U.S. publications covering technology in Beijing. As an entrepreneur, that gap thrilled me. So even as the entire staff of The Information barely filled a tiny San Francisco office, I decided to invest big in Hong Kong just a few months later. Our coverage stood out instantly. Our reporting on Uber’s withdrawal from China was followed by our coverage of the rise of ByteDance, when only a few knew its name . We broke ByteDance’s revenue and product plans annually and revealed the secret deals Tim Cook was striking with the Chinese government, a historic scoop . Our chronicling of China’s crackdown on its own internet companies, was followed by the rise of Shein and Temu and the oft-discussed “decoupling” of the U.S. and China markets. And all that before the current era of the AI cold war with Nvidia at the center , the rise of DeepSeek and, just this week, China’s new strides in chips . Ten years later, even as the U.S. and China tech worlds have changed dramatically, I am in awe of the team that has done this all and keeps on going. And that same coverage gap—the lack of in-depth reporting about China’s tech businesses—still enthralls me. Other news outlets have pulled back from Hong Kong and Beijing, amid real pressures on the press. We take those threats seriously but are pushing ahead independently. This week, we are celebrating another milestone in the bureau: welcoming our first team member in Singapore, Claudia Chong. Jing Yang, our Asia bureau chief, is a force and keeps pushing ahead. Jing reminds me, 10 years after we first opened the bureau, that the urgency of business leaders globally to understand the China market has never been more intense. And our team is on the front lines. It’s funny to look back and remember how it all began: a plane ticket, some phone numbers to try and the naivete that I could pay for things in China with a credit card. And as The Information has grown into an 80-person global news organization, I’m a bit nostalgic for traffic-jammed Beijing days when I managed to make it from Tsinghua University to Xiaomi before staying up way too late meeting with entrepreneurs who didn’t leave the office until midnight. As a reporter and editor, I’ve been lucky to travel the world. But nothing quite compares to my full China immersion, which looking back was one of the most fruitful periods of my professional life. Within a month after my return to the U.S., I was also pregnant with my first son, an ordeal that had taken longer than I had wanted. Two lessons stand out—both for journalists and entrepreneurs. Take the long game and be patient. The Information’s leadership position in Asia tech today dates back more than a decade to my messaging random entrepreneurs on WeChat. While our reporters have done the hard work, without my decision to pack up and get out, I wouldn’t have found the conviction to build a business there—a decision I’ve committed to again and again as the market has changed. And, especially when reporters can direct growing armies of bots to gather all sorts of information from the comfort of their desks, remember to leave your office and wander far. It is then that you are more likely to see something others don’t. And all good stories—and business ideas—come from that.

content:

Child-monitoring apps might need a reboot
Digital harms have become the defining fear of American parents. In response, they’re increasingly turning to content-monitoring apps that scan their children’s texts, photos, emails, and chats, issuing alerts whenever an algorithm flags something it deems dangerous.
These tools have had genuine successes, preventing suicide attempts, intercepting predators, and averting school shootings. But they can also cause harm themselves, from false alarms and unnecessary interventions to damaged trust and anxiety.
Child-safety researchers say better approaches exist.

Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, driven in part by trade disruptions and high natural-gas prices. That’s because natural gas is both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient.
The war in Iran has pushed natural-gas prices higher and disrupted fertilizer trade through the Strait of Hormuz—and its closure could make access harder still for some of the world’s poorest countries.

title: Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
content:
Agriculture relies on fossil fuels. It’s costing us.
Could new fertilizers help combat high prices?
If you’ve had to fill up your vehicle’s gas tank or buy a plane ticket lately, you’ve probably felt the effects of rising fossil-fuel prices. But farmers buying fertilizer for their crops are especially aware of just how far the ripple effects of the conflict in Iran have spread.
Fertilizer prices have been on a roller coaster this year, kicked off in part by trade disruptions and high prices for natural gas, a key ingredient in fertilizer production. Let’s take a closer look at why conventional fertilizer prices are so sky-high, and how a few more climate-friendly alternatives could bring farmers some relief.
As fossil-fuel prices go up, nearly all industries are affected, since most of our economy relies on these fuels to move goods and people around.
But fertilizer is even more intertwined with these fluctuations, because natural gas is used as both an energy source and a chemical input in the production of ammonia, a key fertilizer ingredient. So as natural-gas prices have spiked in recent months because of the war in Iran, fertilizer prices have followed. (It’s worth briefly noting here that fertilizer production is also a major source of greenhouse-gas emissions, accounting for about 2% of the global total.)
Fertilizer trade is being directly affected as well, since about one-third of global seaborne trade in fertilizers passes through the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed to commercial traffic because of the conflict. Access to fertilizer could get worse for some of the poorest countries around the world because of the strait’s closure, according to a report from the World Bank. While the US largely meets demand for nitrogen fertilizers with domestic production, some imports do come from the Persian Gulf.
At one point in April, the price of urea (the most commonly applied fertilizer) climbed above $850 per metric ton. That’s 80% higher than it was before the conflict and the highest level since 2022, when the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the resulting conflict caused fertilizer costs to hit record highs. Prices have come down significantly, but forecasts remain uncertain.
“There’s just this out-of-control supply chain that’s a lot more volatile than it’s ever been,” says Travis Frey, chief technology officer of Pivot Bio, a company making fertilizer with genetically edited microbes. (For more on these microbes, how they work, and what research is still needed, check out my latest story here.)
Pivot says its products are cost-competitive with chemical fertilizers today. And because they don’t use natural gas as an input, they aren’t subject to the same price spikes. When the war in Iran started, Pivot increased the volume it planned to produce, dropped prices, and allowed farmers to lock in prices for three years, Frey says.
That could be a major help for those farmers, because high prices could be here to stay for a while. Some fertilizer prices could remain high through at least 2028, according to a report from CoBank, one of the largest banks for the agriculture industry in the US.
That’s partly because the war has caused long-lasting damage: 31 ammonia plants in the Middle East have been affected or shut down completely. That’s on top of 20 ammonia plants that have been damaged in Russia in recent years.
Ongoing high prices can be extremely challenging for farmers. “The fertilizer price spikes, and because farmers have paper-thin margins, this is a real problem," says Tim Schnabel, founder and CEO of Switch Bioworks, another company working on advanced microbe fertilizers.
Higher costs can help push food prices higher, causing all of us to pay more at the grocery store. (It’s not just fertilizer, by the way. Farmers are also getting hit with wild diesel prices this year.) As long as we’re relying on fertilizers made with fossil fuels, food prices will be tied up with energy prices.
Switch and Pivot are among the companies looking to make alternative fertilizers that use microbes to provide nitrogen to plants. There’s a limit to how much synthetic fertilizers these products can actually replace: Depending on the crop and conditions, Pivot says, its products can replace about 25% of synthetic fertilizer today, and the company hopes to reach 40% to 50% of the total. But these alternatives could be a start to untangling fossil fuels and food.
“We can’t keep doing it like this,” Switch’s Schnabel says. “There’s no way we can build a society where the basis of the food chain depends on fossil fuels.”

title: Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
content:
Scaling agentic AI pilots across the enterprise
As agentic AI moves from pilots to enterprise-wide deployment, orchestration, data, governance, and clear business objectives are becoming critical for scaling, says chief operating officer at NiCE Arun Chandra.
In partnership withNiCE
As agentic AI moves from experimentation toward enterprise deployment, the challenge is figuring out how agents can work together, connect to the systems and data they need, and operate safely across the workflows that run a business. Although agentic AI has been adopted by some 80% of Fortune 500 companies, progress toward meaningful scale remains uneven, with many organizations still working through isolated pilots.
For Arun Chandra, chief operating officer at NiCE, the first step is moving beyond experimentation for its own sake. “Everybody's trying to figure out what can we do with this technology?” he says. But scaling requires a clearer connection to business strategy: Organizations need to define whether they are trying to increase revenue, reduce costs, or pursue another strategic or financial objective. From there, they need to rethink the workflows where agents will operate instead of just layering AI onto existing processes. “The last thing you want to do is to apply AI on an outdated or an inefficient workflow,” Chandra says.
That shift requires organizations to treat agentic AI as a cohesive system. Agents need access to the data, knowledge, and context required to make effective decisions, as well as connections to back-end systems if they are expected to take action. Fragmented information can undermine those capabilities: “The efficacy of these AI agents is purely a function of the context, the knowledge, and the data they can ingest and use,” Chandra says.
The organizational implications are equally noteworthy. Scaling agents can create a new form of fragmentation if teams build isolated systems that don’t connect with one another, while governance, privacy, security, and change management become more important as agents take on more consequential work. Chandra argues that AI agents should ultimately be held to the same standards as human workers, with organizations thinking of their workforce as a combination of humans and AI agents.
Looking ahead, that connected approach could enable agents to work proactively and even communicate with other agents to resolve customer needs. For organizations making the transition from pilots to scale, the priority is not to “boil the ocean,” Chandra says, but to instead build a connected strategy around high-value use cases, workflows, workforce changes, and measurable outcomes.

title: Amazon signs tolling agreement for 50 MW/200 MWh BESS in Australia - Energy Storage
content: US tech giant Amazon has signed a tolling agreement with Anza Power, an Australian subsidiary of US infrastructure investment firm I Squared Capital, for the under-development 50 MW/200 MWh Bairnsdale battery energy storage system (BESS) in Victoria , Australia. The agreement grants Amazon access to energy stored in the Bairnsdale BESS, as well as rights to control charging and discharging and use grid arbitrage. In return, Amazon will pay Sydney-headquartered Anza Power a regular fixed fee without the responsibility of building or maintaining the facility. Significantly, the agreement is a first globally for Amazon for a standalone BESS, and for Australia, represents a first tolling agreement for a non-energy business. Other companies entered into BESS tolling agreements in Australia include gentailers or developers such as EnergyAustralia and Akaysha Energy, which has a 12-year virtual tolling agreement with the Orana BESS. The Bairnsdale BESS will connect directly to the electricity grid as a standalone asset, providing dedicated storage capacity independent of a solar or wind farm. Anza Chief Executive Officer Carlo Frigerio said the agreement reflects the growing demand from major energy purchasers for dedicated storage solutions that support a reliable, low-carbon grid. “Bairnsdale demonstrates our ability to deliver flexible energy infrastructure that respond to the evolving needs of both the market and our customers,” Frigerio said. “We look forward to building on the momentum we have established since launching Anza earlier this year.” Anza and Amazon have other existing agreements including five solar-plus-battery storage power purchasing agreements (PPAs). The Bairnsdale BESS marks the seventh energy agreement signed since Anza was formed and launched by I Squared Capital in January 2026 with a AUD 418.5 million ($300 million) equity commitment through I Squared Capital’s ISQ Growth Markets Infrastructure Fund II. title: D.TRADING, Capalo AI to offer bankable BESS revenue deals - Energy Storage
content: D.TRADING, the energy trading unit of Ukraine’s DTEK Group, and Finnish battery optimizer Capalo AI said they have started working together to offer structured revenue arrangements for battery energy storage and hybrid renewable projects in Europe, combining D.TRADING’s offtake capabilities with Capalo AI’s multi-market trading platform. Under the partnership, D.TRADING will act as the contractual counterparty and offtaker, providing fixed revenue structures and credit support, while Capalo AI will provide market access and trade assets across day-ahead, intraday and ancillary service markets through its Zeus VPP platform, the companies said. Asset owners will enter a single contractual relationship with D.TRADING while drawing on both companies’ capabilities, according to the release. The companies said the offering supports standalone BESS and hybrid renewable projects under multiple commercial structures, including merchant, floor-and-upside-share and tolling agreements. Dmytro Sakharuk, the CEO of D.TRADING, said battery storage is becoming fundamental to how Europe balances its power system and integrates renewable energy, and that the partnership aims to give developers and investors greater revenue certainty without limiting their assets’ market potential. Henri Taskinen, CEO and co-founder of Capalo AI, said the partnership removes a trade-off battery storage projects often face between multi-market optimization and the revenue certainty lenders require, combining D.TRADING’s financial strength with Zeus VPP’s trading capabilities across day-ahead, intraday and ancillary markets. The partnership will initially target battery storage projects in the Balkans, with potential expansion into wider Central, Eastern and South-Eastern European markets where both companies have an established presence, the companies said. Capalo AI manages 1.6 GW of batteries and 460 MWp of solar under its Zeus VPP platform, of which 600 MW and 300 MWp are already live under trading and optimization, according to the company. It operates in six European markets – Bulgaria, Finland, Lithuania, Latvia, Poland and Sweden – and plans to expand into Estonia, Greece, Portugal and Spain in 2026. The Helsinki-based company recently agreed to trade and optimize two Baltic hybrid solar-storage projects for Danish developer European Energy in Lithuania and Latvia, and separately announced a partnership earlier this month with Future Energy to optimize a 56 MW/168 MWh standalone battery storage project in Raseiniai, Lithuania – one of the country’s first commercial battery systems capable of storing and supplying power for up to three hours. The Raseiniai project, delivered by EPC contractor MT Group and valued at more than €30 million ($34.8 million), is expected to reach commercial operation in the first quarter of 2027. title: Floor‑agreement structure anchors 140 MW Alytus BESS deal in Lithuania - Energy Storage
content: Czech-headquartered technology company Second Foundation has partnered with BLEnergy and Shamir Energy on one of Lithuania’s largest standalone battery energy storage systems (BESS), signing an optimization agreement for a to-be-built 140 MW facility in Alytus, Lithuania, south of Kaunas. Commissioning of the project is planned for 2027; BLEnergy told ESS News the Alytus BESS is expected to begin commercial operation in the third quarter of that same year. The company also stated that investment costs for the project are approximately €60 million. Rather than a conventional optimization contract, the parties agreed on a floor agreement – a revenue-protection mechanism where a minimum level of return is guaranteed but allowing for a share in higher returns. This structure is a growing trend in Europe’s battery storage market . The Alytus project combines operational and trading capabilities from the three partners. BL Energy and Shamir Energy bring development and asset-management experience, while Second Foundation contributes algorithmic optimization, along with monetizing experience across energy and ancillary service markets. About the companies involved Israel-based storage developer BLEnergy, part of the Blilious Group, has a project pipeline exceeding 7 GWh in both the Israeli market and several European countries. It has additional facilities in various stages of planning, construction, or operation. The company’s storage systems are based on market-leading technology from CATL . Shamir Energy is also Israel based, developing renewable energy projects with a pipeline of approximately 410 MW of solar, and 2 GWh of storage. Second Foundation operates in nine locations from the USA to Japan, boasting more than 500 analysts, engineers, data scientists, and technology experts managing more than 3 GW of renewable energy – 600 MW of BESS is under construction according to the company. title: Google backs 100 MWh zinc, 280 MWh lithium storage capacity in US - Energy Storage
content: MN8 Energy said it will build “Mammoth Solar,” an 86 MW solar project in Kanawha County, West Virginia, paired with 70 MW/280 MWh of lithium-ion storage and 10 MW/100 MWh of Eos Energy Enterprises’ Z3 zinc-based LDES system. Google will purchase the energy, capacity and clean energy attributes of the project under a long-term agreement, according to MN8. A company spokesperson told ESS News that the project is the same Mammoth Solar development previously permitted in Kanawha County, with battery storage added during the Public Service Commission review process after initial permitting. Google’s participation as offtake partner came after the project was already in development, but the tech giant helped shape the technologies that were ultimately selected. The megawatt allocation for the project’s Eos storage component is drawn directly from MN8 and Eos’ previously announced master supply agreement, said the spokesperson. The project is built on a reclaimed coal mine site. MN8 said it will own and operate the integrated portfolio, which the company says is designed to convert intermittent solar generation into a single dispatchable resource matched to the load profile of Google’s regional data centers, including a planned West Virginia facility. MN8 said the Eos Z3 system is designed to provide 10 hours of discharge duration, extending the availability of solar generation beyond the shorter-duration lithium-ion storage in the portfolio. The company said this marks Google’s first project using Eos’ Z3 technology. The solar component is expected to reach commercial operation in 2028, the lithium-ion storage in 2029 and the Eos LDES system in 2030, MN8 said. The company said the project represents the first commercial-scale LDES deployment in West Virginia. MN8 estimates the project represents up to $350 million in capital investment and will generate approximately $4 million in property tax revenue for the county and local schools over its first 20 years of operation. Construction is expected to create approximately 200 jobs, said the company. Lucia Tian, director of advanced energy technologies at Google, said the company is committed to backing solutions that serve its data center capacity needs while accelerating progress toward cleaner, more affordable energy systems, adding that the collaboration with MN8 and Eos aims to deploy a portfolio of round-the-clock technology solutions to help power its digital infrastructure. Company officials said the project reflects MN8’s approach of building a solution around a customer’s specific energy profile, engineering proven and emerging technologies into a single dispatchable resource. The Z3 system is designed to extend the value of clean generation across more hours, strengthen the overall portfolio and deliver more dependable capacity when the grid needs it most, they said. title: Grenergy completes $475 million sale of Chilean solar-storage project - Energy Storage
content: Grenergy has completed the sale of its 272 MW solar and 1.1 GWh battery storage project in Chile to CVC DIF for an enterprise value of $475 million. The transaction was first announced in September 2025, when Grenergy disclosed a value of up to $475 million and said the transfer was conditional on the asset entering operation. At the time, Gabriela was under construction and expected to reach commercial operation in the first half of 2026. The facility combines 272 MW of solar PV capacity with 1,100 MWh of battery storage. Grenergy announced its energization in February, paving the way for commissioning and completion of the sale. Gabriela is also backed by a 15-year hybrid power purchase agreement (PPA). Construction was financed through a $324 million green loan provided by BNP Paribas, Natixis, Société Générale, Scotiabank, SMBC, Bank of America, BBVA, JPMorgan, KfW IPEX, Rabobank and ICO. Under the terms of the transaction, Grenergy will continue providing operations and maintenance (O&M) services for the assets for five years. Oasis de Atacama is Grenergy’s hybrid solar and storage platform in northern Chile, comprising multiple PV plants paired with battery systems. The company currently plans up to 2.5 GW of solar and 14 GWh of storage across several phases, including Gabriela, Víctor Jara, Quillagua and Elena, with long-term power supply contracts associated with some of the facilities. The Gabriela sale follows Grenergy’s December 2024 sale to ContourGlobal, a KKR-backed company, of the Víctor Jara and Quillagua I and II phases. That transaction covered 451 MW of solar and 2.5 GWh of storage and had a value of up to $962 million. Grenergy said the two transactions together represent around 25% of the Oasis de Atacama platform and have a combined enterprise value of nearly $1.5 billion. The divestments form part of Grenergy’s asset rotation strategy under its 2026-2028 strategic plan, which targets €800 million in proceeds from asset sales during the period. The company updated the plan in May, increasing its planned investment through 2028 to €3.7 billion. It also announced expansions of its Oasis platforms in Chile and the development of Iberian Oasis in Spain. Together, the platforms are expected to reach 5 GW of solar and 22 GWh of storage. title: AI-powered drone system for autonomous PV fault detection - pv magazine Global
content:
A research group from Poland and Spain has developed a novel framework for autonomous unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based inspection of PV installations. The system combines thermal and multispectral imaging with AI-based anomaly detection using multi-frame analysis of drone-acquired imagery.
“The central research problem addressed in this work concerns the automated detection of thermal and visual anomalies using drone-acquired imagery,” the researchers said. “Importantly, the thermal module is used for relative anomaly detection rather than absolute temperature measurement. Thermal images are treated as visual patterns, and anomalies are confirmed through multi-frame consistency across different viewing angles.”
The researchers developed a custom hexacopter equipped with a FLIR Boson 640 radiometric thermal camera and a MicaSense Altum multispectral camera. The FLIR camera operates in the 7.5–13.5 μm long-wave infrared range, has a resolution of 640 × 512 pixels at 30 Hz, and offers thermal sensitivity below 50 mK. The MicaSense Altum simultaneously captures RGB, thermal, and multispectral imagery. The aircraft and sensor payload were powered by dedicated power supplies, enabling flight times of approximately 25 minutes.
Using this setup, the researchers conducted multiple autonomous flight campaigns over a small residential PV installation and a large industrial-scale facility under varying atmospheric conditions. The flights took place during daylight hours at ambient temperatures ranging from 12 C to 22 C, mostly under clear or partly cloudy skies and with wind speeds below 12 m/s.
The UAV operated at altitudes ranging from 18 m to 30 m to maintain a ground sampling distance of approximately 2.5 cm to 4.0 cm per pixel. The researchers also adjusted flight speed and track spacing to ensure sufficient image overlap.
The researchers used imagery collected during the flight campaigns to build the model dataset. It comprised 1,950 proprietary flight images, 190 images from the publicly available Kaggle “Solar Panel Images” repository, and 260 laboratory images depicting controlled contamination.
They first removed blurred, overexposed, excessively noisy, and irrelevant frames before normalizing the remaining images and segmenting and cropping individual PV modules.
The researchers manually labeled anomalous modules as exhibiting dust, sand, bird droppings, or hotspots, while classifying normal modules as clean. They allocated 81.25% of the images to training, 7.92% to validation, and 10.83% to testing.
The researchers then compared four convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures: EfficientNet-B0, ResNet18, MobileNetV3-Small, and RegNet-Y16GF.
EfficientNet-B0 delivered the best overall performance, with precision of 0.903, recall of 0.907, a macro F1 score of 0.904, and a weighted F1 score of 0.927. The F1 score represents the balance between precision and recall.
Performance varied by anomaly class. The model achieved precision, recall, and F1 scores of 1.000 for both hotspots and clean modules. It recorded an F1 score of 0.907 for sand and 0.889 for bird droppings. Dust proved the most difficult anomaly to identify, with precision of 0.711, recall of 0.751, and an F1 score of 0.732.
“The modular design of the system enables straightforward extension toward coordinated multi-UAV operation and enhanced multi-sensor fusion, offering a pathway toward next-generation, high-throughput PV-monitoring platforms,” the researchers concluded. “The methodological transparency introduced in this work – including detailed sensor specification, dataset composition, and anomaly-classification procedures – ensures that the system can be reliably reproduced and further developed in future studies.”
The researchers presented the framework in “
Automated UAV thermal imaging and AI-based detection of hotspots and surface contamination in photovoltaic panels
,” published in
Measurement
. The research team included scientists from Rzeszow University of Technology in Poland and Spain’s
Valencia Polytechnic University

title: Brazil approves law linking data center incentives to renewable energy use - pv magazine Global
content:
On Tuesday, Brazil’s Federal Senate approved Bill 278/2026, establishing the Special Taxation Regime for Data Center Services (Redata). The text, approved without substantive changes to the version passed by the Chamber of Deputies, now goes to the president for sanction.
Among the conditions for accessing the tax benefits, data centers must meet their contracted electricity demand through supply agreements or self-generation using renewable or low-emission energy sources.
The Senate’s amendment was primarily a change in wording. The text replaced “clean or renewable sources” with “renewable or low-emission sources,” broadening the language of the original proposal and leaving the applicable criteria to be defined in subsequent regulations. The Senate cites solar and wind as examples of renewable sources, and hydropower, biomass and biogas as low-emission sources.
The requirement puts electricity procurement at the center of Brazil’s policy to attract investment in digital infrastructure and could add to demand already growing in the country’s free electricity market.
A survey by Clean Energy Latin America (CELA) identified 11 long-term contracts between renewable energy generators and data centers in Brazil from 2021 to 2024, totaling 330 MW and approximately BRL 7.7 billion ($1.4 billion) in transactions. Seven of the deals were structured under the self-generation model, while four were power purchase agreements (PPAs).
Solar and wind gain new demand potential
The combination of growing digital infrastructure and renewable energy procurement requirements could expand the market for generation projects developed to serve large loads.
For data center developers, long-term contracts with generators can link the expansion of computing capacity to a more predictable electricity procurement strategy. For generators, large, high-consumption loads can provide significant offtake opportunities for new projects.
The trend is already emerging in Brazil. According to CELA, the contracts identified through 2024 involved solar and wind generation and were structured primarily through self-generation arrangements and PPAs in Brazil’s Free Contracting Environment (ACL).
Self-generation and PPAs
Self-generation is likely to remain relevant for large-scale projects, particularly where consumers can establish partnerships with generation projects.
PPAs, meanwhile, allow data centers to contract electricity directly from generators over long periods, providing greater cost and supply predictability while supporting investment in new generation capacity.
CELA’s survey indicates the potential scale of the market. The 330 MWavg contracted by data centers from 2021 to 2024 represented approximately BRL 7.7 billion in transactions.
Incentives and obligations
Redata suspends federal taxes on equipment and components acquired domestically or imported for use in data centers. The suspension covers import duties, PIS/Cofins, PIS/Cofins-Import and the Tax on Industrialized Products (IPI), and will apply for five years.
In return, participating companies must allocate at least 10% of their installed data processing, storage and handling capacity to the Brazilian market; comply with sustainability criteria; meet contracted electricity demand through supply agreements or self-generation using renewable or low-emission sources; comply with water-efficiency limits for cooling systems; and invest in Brazil an amount equivalent to 2% of the value of products acquired under the tax incentive.
For the electricity sector, the most significant potential impact comes from the combination of growing digital loads and the requirement to procure electricity from renewable or low-emission sources.
If sanctioned, Redata could strengthen the role of data centers as a new class of large-scale electricity consumers in Brazil and increase demand for generation projects, long-term contracts and flexibility solutions as the country’s digital infrastructure expands.

title: Data Centres and the clean energy imperative: Powering India’s digital economy sustainably - pv magazine Global
content:
India’s digital economy is entering a phase in which computing growth and power infrastructure can no longer be planned separately. Artificial intelligence, cloud services, digital payments and data localisation are increasing demand for computing capacity, while data centres are becoming larger and more power intensive.
India illustrates the scale of this shift. Data-centre capacity increased fourfold from about 375 MW in 2020 to around 1,500 MW by 2025. The Economic Survey 2025–26 cites industry estimates of around 4 GW by 2030. The IEA also expects India’s electricity demand to grow by an average 6.4% a year between 2026 and 2030. Data centres will therefore expand within a power system already responding to industrialisation, cooling demand and wider electrification.
The clean-energy imperative is becoming central to where data centres are located, how quickly they can be commissioned and whether they can operate reliably at scale.
Power is becoming part of the investment case
A data-centre asset creates value only when sufficient, reliable power is available to support computing capacity. That makes time-to-power a strategic investment variable alongside land, fibre connectivity and construction economics.
Grid capacity, connection timelines, substation requirements, transmission constraints, renewable sourcing and future load growth need to be assessed before development assumptions become fixed. A location that appears attractive can become commercially difficult if network reinforcement takes years or if the power architecture cannot scale with demand.
Renewable generation and storage can often be deployed modularly and, under suitable conditions, on shorter timelines than large conventional generation or major network reinforcement. Actual delivery schedules, however, still depend on site readiness, permitting and grid connectivity.
Annual renewable-energy procurement can reduce the carbon intensity of electricity consumption, but it does not guarantee clean power every hour. Solar output is concentrated during daylight; wind varies by location and season; and grid congestion can emerge when reliability matters most. Data centres operate continuously and have very limited tolerance for interruption.
The requirement is an integrated portfolio: renewable generation, battery energy storage systems, firm grid supply, substations, transmission capacity and backup arrangements. Depending on the facility’s criticality, renewable energy supported by storage can form a significant part of the supply mix, while firm grid supply and standby generation provide additional resilience.
Data-centre technology is also changing rapidly. Higher-density computing, evolving cooling requirements and compressed development schedules mean power planning must begin earlier.
Reliability and decarbonisation must be designed together
Battery energy storage can improve resilience while shifting renewable generation, managing demand peaks and supporting power quality.
The engineering challenge is to ensure these technologies operate as one system. Storage duration, degradation, dispatch strategy, protection settings, backup architecture and grid-code compliance influence performance and investment returns. Decisions taken in isolation can create costly interface problems later.
Engineering confidence and independent technical assurance
The scale and speed of data-centre development can create pressure to commit capital before energy risks are fully understood. That makes independent engineering and technical advisory important.
The approach starts with the investment question rather than the equipment list: what power is required, how quickly can it be connected, how should renewable generation and storage be configured, where are the interface risks, and can the system expand without compromising reliability?
Independent technical oversight helps keep these decisions aligned with long-term availability, bankability and asset performance. Technical due diligence, Owner’s Engineering, grid studies, EPCM, quality assurance and operational performance review are most effective when they operate as one connected lifecycle framework.
India can build a cleaner digital advantage
India combines renewable resources with a deep engineering base and capability to execute digital and power infrastructure at scale. Developers, utilities, investors and technology companies need credible demand forecasts so grid connections, renewable supply, storage and network infrastructure can be planned ahead of congestion.
India’s digital economy will ultimately be supported by physical systems: substations, transmission lines, renewable plants, batteries and control platforms. If these systems are planned with the same precision and urgency as the computing infrastructure they serve, data-centre growth can strengthen both economic competitiveness and the clean-energy transition.
The clean-energy imperative is becoming part of the core engineering and investment logic of India’s digital economy for the decade ahead.

title: Hiring more women deemed a remedy to energy transition workforce shortages - pv magazine Global
content:
Based on industry surveys, shortages in critical energy transition occupations, can be improved with better employment strategies and culture, as well as addressing insufficient skills development to meet the pace of change.
Powering Skills Organisation’s (PSO’s) estimated target of 42,000 new qualified workers being required, has found workforce pressures beyond the demands of an energy transition now top heavy with rapid growth in artifiical intelligence (AI) data centre developments, is at risk of being derailed by skilled worker shortages.
Australia-headquartered energy sector workforce policy entity PSO’s High Load, Short Supply 2026 Targeted
Workforce Update
report says workforce growth is also constrained by limited training capacity and business confidence.
“As revealed by engagement with more than 400 employers, employees, training providers, industry bodies, unions and apprentices through PSO’s 2026 energy skills and workforce survey, and national roadshows,” the report cites.
“Regional stakeholders also identified persistent challenges relating to workforce mobility, training access, supervision capacity and thin labour markets. Across the engagement, stakeholders consistently called for structural reforms to support stronger workforce growth, mobility and coordination.”
Among surveyed employers, 55% continued to carry vacancies in the past 12 months, and 52% had positions unfilled for longer than six months.
Having only one pathway into the licensed electrical workforce via a Cert III in Electrotechnology, is hindered further by school leavers abandoning apprenticeships early, being underprepared by the education system for the literacy and numeracy demands of the training.
PSOs research found 59% of electrotechnology apprenticeships cancellations occur in the first year of study, and 26% in the second.
Completion rates however are at 70% and the larger barrier is the creation of apprenticeship opportunities, the report says.
The largest burden for apprentice employment falls to small and medium electrical contracting businesses, which in term boilds down to the practicalities of commercial viability.
Workplace culture can be a constraint where significant talent pools, including
, First Nations peoples and culturally and linguistically diverse communities are underutilised.
PSO has developed a solutions-focussed framework, outlined in the report, which addresses four recurrent themes to have emerged from its survey of the energy sector.
The Four Cs framework covers capacity, which defines the scale of the workforce required, capability covering the skills needed by that workforce, culture that could offer inclusive and safe workplaces to attract and retain talent, and confidence, which opens the door to investment and
certainty

title: Electric Hydrogen to supply electrolysers in Karratha, Western Australia
content:
Electric Hydrogen to supply electrolysers in Karratha, Western Australia
Perdaman’s Project Helios secures agreement for 120 tons per day of renewable hydrogen
Projected to be Australia’s largest domestic ammonia and urea manufacturing facility, Perdaman’s Project Ceres is located in Karratha, Western Australia. With production targets of 2.3 million tons of urea per year, using gas supplied by Woodside and offtake agreements with Incitec Pivot, the project also utilises 5MW of solar energy.
Towards decarbonised ammonia production, Perdaman’s Project Helios is in charge of delivering 1GW of solar power to produce at least 120 tons per day of renewable hydrogen for ammonia production at Project Ceres. In the most recent news, Perdaman has announced Electric Hydrogen (EH2) as the preferred electrolyser supplier. This agreement follows a successful pre-FEED partnership.
When we began Project Ceres, our vision was to strengthen Australia’s manufacturing future. Project Helios is the next step in that journey, advancing the decarbonisation of Australian industry through clean, Australian-made hydrogen.
Vikas Rambal, Chairman, Perdaman in his organisation’s press release, 17 Aug 2026
Perdaman is building a state-of-the-art urea production facility on the Burrup Peninsula near Karratha. Electric Hydrogen’s economically viable large scale HYPRplant electrolysis solution will enable Perdaman to address Australia’s critical need for low-carbon, domestically produced fertilizer. We’re excited to partner with Perdaman on this important mission
Raffi Garabedian, CEO, Electric Hydrogen in Perdaman’s press release, 17 Aug 2026
Perdaman is an multi-national company, based in Western Australia with expertise in numerous sectors including fertiliser production and sustainable energy solutions. Perdaman is investing AU$6.5 billion in Project Ceres aiming to develop and support Australia’s sovereign fertiliser industry and food security. The Australia Government is backing the work with AU$475 million in loans. Perdaman was one of four companies the West Australian state government allocated land to with the vision of a Pilbara Hydrogen Hub.
EH2, based in Massachusetts, USA, specialises in decarbonisation at the 100 MW-scale with its modular HYPRPlant electrolyser that produces renewable, low-cost hydrogen.

title: Ammobia and Lummus partner to licence and deploy new ammonia production technology
content:
Ammobia and Lummus partner to licence and deploy new ammonia production technology
“Haber Bosch 2.0” ready to commercialise
Texas-based Lummus Technology and California-based Ammobia have signed a new agreement to licence and deploy Ammobia’s next-generation ammonia production technology. The technology, dubbed “Haber-Bosch 2.0”, delivers a capital-efficient synthesis loop (synloop), low-cost ammonia production, and versatility in energy source. The modular design presents the opportunity for medium-sized ammonia production plants to decrease the global reliance on traditional megaprojects in addition to retrofitting options.
Lummus and Ammobia are initially targeting 50-500 tons per day ammonia production plant operators looking to supply low-cost ammonia to sectors including maritime fuels and in-demand power generation.
Lummus will help de-risk and accelerate the roll out of Ammobia’s production process with an established customer base and globally demonstrated expertise in the engineering and technology aspects of developing process technologies. This is Lummus’ first venture into ammonia technology, which complements and integrates with its feedstock flexible hydrogen portfolio providing varied and flexible decarbonisation choices for customers.
Ammobia changes the economics of producing ammonia from any energy source and does it in modules rather than the world-scale plants that have defined this industry for a century. Customers can add capacity through a greenfield project or an upgrade to an existing operating site. Lummus brings the engineering rigor, project delivery, and global relationships required to deploy it, which lets Ammobia stay focused on advancing the core process. Together we can make ammonia’s newest applications, from resilient power to clean maritime fuel, commercially viable.
Karen Baert, Co-founder and CEO, Ammobia in her organisation’s press release, 27 Aug 2026
We have a long track record of partnering with innovators to scale breakthrough technologies that address the evolving needs of the global energy market. Ammobia’s technology is an important addition to Lummus’ portfolio and a leap forward for the industry. This cutting-edge solution has the power to transform ammonia production to be more economical and lower carbon, support emissions reductions in the shipping industry, and significantly reduce project costs.
Leon de Bruyn, President and CEO, Lummus Technology, in Ammobia’s press release, 27 Aug 2026
Ammobia’s technology boasts low-temperature (300°C) and relatively low-pressure (20 bar) ammonia production. The company integrates low-temperature ammonia catalysts with solid sorbents for ammonia separation for up to 80% single pass conversion in its reactor and predicts scale up to 50 kilograms per day plant (TRL 6) in 2026.

title: Enapter wins electrolyzer order from US drone manufacturer | Hydrogen Tech World.com
content:
The order comprises units from its 4.1 series of AEM electrolyzers and is scheduled for delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026.
The AEM modules will be integrated into mobile, all-terrain refueling systems that generate hydrogen directly at the point of operation from water and solar power, without a grid connection. This approach removes the need to transport and store hydrogen in large compressed gas cylinders, which has been among the main obstacles to operating hydrogen-powered drones in remote areas.
According to Enapter, hydrogen propulsion gives drones significantly longer flight and mission times compared with battery-electric propulsion, along with rapid refueling capability.
The order is structured as a pilot project. Enapter said it opens up a field of application in which the modular design of AEM technology is well suited, citing a compact footprint, robust operation, and the ability to scale hydrogen production by adding further modules.
Dr Jürgen Laakmann, Chief Executive Officer of Enapter , said: “This order underlines how far the applications of our technology reach beyond classic industrial use. In this case hydrogen is generated flexibly where it is needed – free of complex supply chains and of any fuel logistics. That is exactly what our modular, low-maintenance AEM technology was built for. We see considerable growth potential in mobile refuelling solutions and are pleased to be developing this field together with a technologically leading customer.”
Enapter said the market for drones with long range and long flight times is growing strongly worldwide, and that the pilot project opens up a field of application with scalable demand for the company.

title: CRAFT低温系统6 kW@4.5 K氦制冷机调试成功
content:
2026-09-03 15:20 来源：中国科学院等离子体物理研究所
CRAFT低温系统
近日，CRAFT磁体平台氦制冷系统建设取得重要进展。CRAFT低温系统6kW@4.5K氦制冷机主体现场调试及性能测试顺利完成，各项指标均达到设计验收要求。
调试工作重点围绕氦制冷机冷箱的制冷性能、液化能力、控制系统、安全联锁以及关键低温设备运行状态等内容展开系统验证。验收测试期间，氦制冷机在设计工况下完成了连续12小时稳定运行，同时实现了6kW@4.5K+50K@GHe的制冷能力。除设计工况外，项目团队还开展了氦液化工况性能测试，相关温度、压力、流量、加热功率以及杜瓦液位等参数均保持在相应运行范围内，这一结果验证了氦制冷机在复杂负荷条件下的制冷能力和运行稳定性，为后续根据超导负载需求灵活调整运行模式提供了重要技术基础。在性能测试基础上，项目团队对氦制冷机安全功能进行了验证，模拟了停电或紧急停机后的系统重启、真空系统运行等工况，进一步检验了冷箱及相关子系统之间的协同控制、安全保护和故障恢复能力，为系统长期连续、稳定可靠运行提供了保障。
6kW@4.5K级氦制冷机是CRAFT低温系统的重要核心子系统。此次主体性能调试成功，全面检验了氦制冷机在大制冷量、液化等不同运行模式下的综合性能，以及冷箱、压缩机站、控制系统和相关辅助系统的协同运行能力。这一重要节点标志着CRAFT低温系统由设备建设安装阶段进一步迈向系统联调和应用运行阶段。该系统将为超导磁体及相关低温实验装置的系统联调、性能验证和稳定运行提供可靠的深低温条件，并为大型超导磁体、先进低温技术及相关重大科研装备开展实验研究提供重要基础支撑。
此次调试成功，得益于团队在低温工程、自动控制等多学科领域的协同攻关，也为后续承担更大规模低温系统建设与运行任务奠定了人才和技术基础，进一步验证了等离子体所大科学团队在大型氦制冷装备集成、调试及运行保障方面的综合技术能力。

title: 秦山核电格栅清理机械手臂完成大修验证
content:
秦山核电格栅清理机械手臂完成大修验证
秦山核电维修四处机械团队自主研发的“无人机智能巡检+机械臂自动清理”设备——格栅清理机械手臂，近日在秦二厂312大修中完成现场验证。该设备面向海水系统取水格栅清理场景，可将原本依赖人工进入深井的作业方式，转变为地面远程监控下的无人化作业。
取水格栅是核电厂冷却水系统的重要屏障，其通畅状态关系机组运行稳定。传统清理方式中，作业人员需要进入地下二十余米的狭窄井道，在受限空间内开展检查和清理，存在作业强度大、效率低以及高处坠落、缺氧窒息等安全风险。
针对这一运维难点，秦山核电维修四处机械团队开展了为期8个多月的技术攻关，形成了集无人机巡检、智能识别和机械臂清理于一体的作业系统。作业前端由搭载高清传感设备的无人机完成格栅区域扫描和识别，生成可视化作业图谱;随后，机械臂依据回传数据自主规划路径，执行抓取、清运等操作，技术人员在地面进行远程监控和指挥。
在秦二厂312大修试用过程中，该机械手臂及时发现一处SEC格栅条破损缺陷，为后续处理争取了时间，降低了大修期间相关安全风险。现场验证结束后，研发团队对设备性能进行了评估，并梳理出后续优化方向。
据介绍，该系统应用后，作业人员无需进入深井，可从源头减少受限空间高风险作业;同时，原本可能需要数小时的清理工作，可压缩至数分钟内完成，有助于降低相关作业对机组运行和检修组织的影响。
此次验证表明，秦山核电在复杂环境下无人机稳定巡检、狭小空间机械臂精准操作等方面取得了阶段性应用成果。该技术路线也可为市政排水深井、大型水利设施、化工能源等存在受限空间作业需求的场景提供参考。
